hints: Think about acidity first, as a more acidic O-H means a faster, more vigorous reaction with sodium.
Water reacts more violently with sodium than ethanol does, so ethanol must be the weaker acid with the stronger conjugate base.
Consider how the ethyl group pushes electrons toward the oxygen and what that extra electron density does to base strength.
walkthrough:
**Compare the reactions with sodium**

Think of sodium with O-H compounds as an acid-metal reaction. The more acidic the O-H, the faster and more vigorous the release of hydrogen.

$$2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$$
$$2\text{Na} + 2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$

**Decide which is more acidic, water or ethanol**

In practice, water fizzes violently with sodium while ethanol reacts much more gently and slowly. So water is the stronger acid and ethanol is the weaker acid, meaning ethanol is harder to deprotonate.

**Link acid strength to base strength**

Remember the golden rule: a weak acid gives a strong conjugate base. Since $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is weaker than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, its conjugate base $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ must be stronger than $\text{OH}^-$.

**Explain it with the inductive effect**

The ethyl group $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-$ is electron-donating by the positive inductive (+I) effect. It pushes electron density onto the already negative oxygen, making the charge more intense and concentrated.

This destabilises the anion and makes it more eager to accept a proton, so ethoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide.

options.A: Incorrect. Sodium reacts more vigorously and faster with water than with ethanol at the same temperature. This is because water is more acidic, so this statement has the rates the wrong way round.
options.B: Correct. Ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so its conjugate base is stronger. The ethyl group donates electrons (+I effect) to oxygen, increasing electron density on O and making CH3CH2O- more ready to accept H+ than OH-.
options.C: Incorrect. There is no delocalisation in ethoxide. The negative charge is localised on the oxygen atom because the ethyl group has no pi system or lone-pair acceptor to spread the charge over.
options.D: Incorrect. It is harder, not easier, to deprotonate ethanol. Ethanol (pKa about 16) is less acidic than water (pKa about 15.7), which is exactly why its reaction with sodium is slower.
